title: Living ashtpadi 10
hook: seeing the countless makes our worries smaller
tomorrow: Ashtpadi 11, salok: the doer of all

segments.voice: Yesterday, all in His creation: the proud and the lost, counted too, and only the Creator knows it. Your line was all in the play. Did you set the gavel down? Today, we live ashtpadi ten. Day four hundred seventy-seven.

It's two in the morning, and a worry has taken over the whole room. An email you shouldn't have sent. A bill. A test result. Lying in bed, it feels like the biggest thing in the universe. Then you get up for water, glance out the window, and there, if the sky is clear, are the stars. Hundreds you can see. Billions you can't. The worry doesn't vanish. But it shrinks, a little, to its real size. Astronomers didn't invent that feeling, and neither did poets. Ashtpadi ten knew it too.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING, ONE WORRY.` → `A GLANCE AT THE STARS.` → `THE WORRY FINDS ITS REAL SIZE.`

segments.voice: After counting the seekers and the lost, ashtpadi ten widens out even further. Its drumbeat, kaee kot, many millions, moves from people to worlds. One stanza says: many millions are the sources of life and the regions of the earth. Many millions are the skies and the brahmands. Brahmand is a universe, literally the cosmic egg, a whole world-system. Many millions of universes. Guru Nanak said something similar in Japji, which we read last year: worlds below worlds, hundreds of thousands of skies above skies, and people grow tired searching for the limit. Sikhs often point out how naturally these lines sit beside what modern astronomers describe: a universe with more galaxies than anyone can count. The Granth isn't a science textbook, and nobody needs it to be. But the picture is the same in spirit: vast, uncountable, beyond any edge we can find. Now, what does it mean to live this? The outline puts it simply: seeing the countless makes our worries smaller. Not unimportant. Smaller. Your worry is real, and it's yours, and the Creator of many millions of universes still holds it. But it's not the center of everything. That's the gift of ashtpadi ten. It takes you outside on a clear night and says: look how big this is. Look how much is being held. Now, put your worry down for a moment, and see what size it really is.
screen: `FROM PEOPLE TO WORLDS.` · `BRAHMAND: A WHOLE UNIVERSE.` · `JAPJI: SKIES ABOVE SKIES.` · `NOT UNIMPORTANT, JUST SMALLER.` · then, large: `SMALLER WORRIES.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at the stars. If it's night and you can, step outside or go to a window. If it's daytime, close your eyes and picture the darkest, clearest sky you've ever seen. Let your eyes go from one star to the next. Then think: behind every one, more. Let one worry come into your mind, and place it under that sky. Notice its size now. If you pray, you can hand it over to the One who holds the many millions. The bell holds the time.
Living ashtpadi ten. Many millions of skies and universes: seeing the countless gives our worries back their real size.
Your line: smaller worries. Tonight, before bed, look at the sky for one minute, or picture it, and let your biggest worry stand under it. Day four hundred seventy-seven.

screen: `DAY 477 COUNTS.` → `ASHTPADI 10, LIVED.` → `TOMORROW: ASHTPADI 11, SALOK: THE DOER OF ALL.`

howItsDone: Sikhs read the 'kaee kot' stanzas of Sukhmani Sahib, and Japji's lines on countless worlds, as hymns of wonder that put personal troubles in the setting of a vast creation.

original.note: Gurmukhi: brahmand, a universe, literally the cosmic egg; ashtpadi ten counts them by the millions.

trapdoor: what you thought: a big universe makes us meaningless.
what it means: it shrinks the worry to its real size, while the Creator still holds it.
what a scholar hears: brahmand (Sanskrit brahmaanda, Brahma's egg) is the Puranic term for a world-system; Gurbani uses it, with khand and akaas, for the plurality of worlds also found in Japji 22.
